extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media professionals, and readers concerned with journalistic ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Critique of a magazine feature that lays out expectations for verification, editorial oversight, sourcing, anonymity, apologies, and leadership responsibility in magazine journalism. Aimed at improving how reporters and editors handle serious allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify allegations before presenting as fact
rubrics_metrics.description: "Just not, by dint of what journalists or authorities were able to uncover, anything like the heinous account that Rolling Stone omnisciently presented as fact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present uncorroborated allegations as established fact; reporters and editors must confirm details through independent verification or official findings before stating them definitively. The Rolling Stone piece is given as an example of presenting an unverified, sensational narrative as fact and thereby failing journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confirmation bias; don't shop for locations to fit a narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: "Erdely started from the belief that campus rape is a problem ... She was shopping for locations to illustrate what she thought was a crisis, and landed on the University of Virginia as a perfect locale ... The central story ... fit too neatly into Erdely's view for her to consider seriously the kind of reporting that would be needed to confirm the details."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should not begin reporting with a predetermined narrative and then select sources or locations to confirm it. Instead, remain open to evidence that may complicate or contradict a thesis and pursue the reporting necessary to confirm key details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must be active partners in verification
rubrics_metrics.description: "Her editors were along for the ride. Erdely ... had signaled to editors that the narration of the gang rape was from Jackie’s point of view."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not passively accept a reporter's framing (e.g., 'from X's point of view') as a substitute for corroboration. Editorial oversight requires pushing for independent sources, fact-checking, and scrutiny of claims—editors share responsibility for what is published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not serve as a megaphone; exercise editorial gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: "The magazine is not a megaphone, for anyone to grab. It determines what to publish in its own pages and on its site."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications must exercise judgment about what to amplify. Simply relaying a powerful or emotional account without the necessary verification abdicates editorial responsibility and risks spreading falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting pseudonyms requires extra verification
rubrics_metrics.description: "Erdely’s editors were active partners in the decisions to grant pseudonyms and to fail to seek out sources to verify or disprove the grave accusations that Jackie made."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reporter or publication grants anonymity or pseudonyms, that heightened protection for a source demands additional effort to corroborate the claims. Anonymity should not be used as a shield to avoid the verification that serious allegations require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full apologies should explicitly address harmed parties
rubrics_metrics.description: "Her mea culpa lacked any direct apology to the campus chapter of Phi Kappa Psi, the fraternity that her article singled out ... They deserved an apology from her. They did not receive it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting errors harm identifiable people or organizations, responsible apologies should explicitly acknowledge and address the specific parties harmed rather than only offering general regret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership must accept responsibility rather than blame sources
rubrics_metrics.description: "Jann Wenner ... denounced Jackie as 'a really expert fabulist storyteller' ... Wrong again. This sits at Rolling Stone's doorstep."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and senior leaders should take responsibility for editorial failures instead of shifting blame to sources. Leadership accountability is part of maintaining institutional journalistic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not privilege emotional narrative over factual integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The magazine made the decision to defend Jackie’s emotional state at all costs. In this case, the decision ended up costing Rolling Stone its journalistic integrity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empathy for sources and attention to emotional truth must be balanced with rigorous fact-gathering; defending an emotional account 'at all costs' can undermine credibility and integrity if factual claims are not substantiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately represent the extent and nature of your sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Erdely said ... that she had talked to almost all of Jackie’s friends. That appears to be untrue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should not overstate or misrepresent who they spoke to or how many corroborating sources they have. Precise, honest descriptions of sourcing are essential for credibility and for editors and readers to evaluate the strength of a story.
